title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab
talk_summary: Felipe Blanes (Amazon AGI Lab) argues that static benchmarks create a 'benchmark illusion' and that teams should run an eval flywheel: define customer-defined success, capture production signals plus direct customer conversations, categorize gaps into model/engineering/product buckets, and prioritize fixes. He adds that reliability is a trust cliff (80% means 'I must still babysit it', ~90% means 'I can hand it over') and that transparently publishing what the product cannot do builds more trust than higher benchmark scores.

takeaways.technique: Eval flywheel fed by production failures, not synthetic imagination
takeaways.what_they_do: They treat evals as a continuously refreshed loop: derive eval scenarios from real production/customer signals rather than only synthetic data, then re-run the loop as fast as possible so the eval suite gets smarter every week.

takeaways.technique: Categorize every gap into model / engineering / product before assigning
takeaways.what_they_do: When diagnosing failures they sort signals into three buckets — model failures (feed evals), engineering/harness bugs (normal bug fixing), and product/positioning gaps — then route each to the right team for prioritization.
takeaways.evidence_quote: inputs about your model ... inputs to your engineering team ... also on the product side

takeaways.technique: Reliability trust cliff — target hand-off grade, not 'mostly works'
takeaways.what_they_do: They observed customers treat sub-90% reliability as net-negative work (build it AND monitor it AND fix it manually), while ~90%+ flips the message to 'I can hand this over'; reliability is effectively binary for adoption.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when you get to a point around 90% reliability the message changes
takeaways.numbers: 80% reliability reads as untrustworthy; ~90% reads as trustworthy/hand-off-able

takeaways.technique: Customer-journey stages to decide what to build next
takeaways.what_they_do: They map customer signals to four journey stages — use-case discovery, early-adopter 'what's possible', scaling 'hero use case' patterns, and future product gaps — and use the stage to decide which signals matter now.
takeaways.evidence_quote: each customer will have their own journey using my product ... my customer evolves as they use my product
transparent on product limitation increase trust more than higher benchmarks

takeaways.technique: Cache successful trajectories, fall back to model on miss
takeaways.what_they_do: A customer-driven feature: cache agent trajectories and replay them instead of always doing inference; on failure, fall back to the live model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we cache trajectories. If it fail, we just fall back to the model. So we optimize the cost for them
